Read and write your own Arya lists from another app or a script, and take your data with you. The same personal API token that the agent connector uses works here. Make one in Arya under Settings › Use Arya in another AI app. The code shows once; a new code replaces it. Base URL: https://arya.teamnightshift.org/api/v1 The same guide, shorter, is the public page at /developers, with a five-minute quickstart in curl, Python and JavaScript. The interactive reference (try the calls from the browser) is at /developers/reference. /api/v1 is frozen. Changes after it ships are additive only: new endpoints, new optional fields, new response fields. Clients must ignore fields they do not know. The machine-readable schema is at /api/v1/openapi.json (public, no token needed). export ARYA=https://arya.teamnightshift.org/api/v1 export TOKEN=... # your code Every call sends Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN. The token reaches only your own account's data. Cookie sign-in does not work on /api/v1.

A list is {id, name, stores, open_count}. open_count is the number of items not yet checked. The id unfiled is "Everything else": the items that sit on no named list. An item is {id, name, qty, unit, checked, aisle, added_at, list_id}. aisle is the department you set yourself, else null. Arya's own guess from the name is not part of the API. added_at is a UTC time. It is null for items added before the API existed and for items Arya suggested. checked is for the current shopping cycle, as in the app. An item sits on one list at a time.

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $ARYA/lists # [{"id":"unfiled","name":"Everything else","stores":[],"open_count":1}, # {"id":"l-1a2b3c4d","name":"Costco","stores":["Costco"],"open_count":3}]
The list, plus items. curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $ARYA/lists/l-1a2b3c4d

Add items. Send items (structured) or text (free text), not both. At most 50 items per call. # structured: a name, or an object with qty, unit and aisle curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"items":["oat milk",{"name":"rice","qty":2,"unit":"kg","aisle":"Pantry"}]}' \ $ARYA/lists/l-1a2b3c4d/items # free text: split the way the app splits typed lists ("eggs x 3, bread") curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"text":"milk\neggs x 3\nbread"}' $ARYA/lists/l-1a2b3c4d/items Reply: {"added": 2, "already": 1, "already_names": [{"name": "milk", "list": "Costco"}], "also_on": [], "skipped": [], "items": [ ... ]} already: names that were already on this list. They are not added twice. also_on: names that are already on a different list. The API does not move them and does not add them to this list; the reply says where they are. To move one, PATCH its list_id. (In the app a person can keep an item on more than one list. The API shows such an item once, under its main list, and its ticks there are the main list's.) skipped: pieces of text that were not items (a bare number). A line with a sentence in it is skipped whole, so no piece of it is added. items: the items now on the list for the names you sent. text is split by fixed rules. The API makes no model calls.

Change any of checked, qty, unit, list_id (a list id, unfiled, or null for Everything else), aisle ("" clears it). Nothing changes if any field is bad. curl -s -X PATCH -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"checked":true}' $ARYA/items/manual-milk curl -s -X PATCH -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"list_id":"l-9f8e7d6c","qty":2,"aisle":"Dairy"}' $ARYA/items/manual-milk Reply: the item.
curl -s -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $ARYA/items/manual-milk # {"deleted":"manual-milk"}

json (the default) is {"list": {id, name, stores}, "items": [...]}. text is a checklist, one item per line: ☐ rice 2 kg, ☐ eggs x 12, ☑ milk. csv has this header and these columns, in this order: name,qty,unit,checked,department,list rice,2,kg,false,Pantry,Costco checked is true or false. A cell that starts with = + - @ gets a leading apostrophe so a spreadsheet does not run it as a formula. Import removes it. curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$ARYA/lists/l-1a2b3c4d/export?format=csv" > costco.csv

Send the file as the request body. The format is csv when the Content-Type contains csv, else text. ?format=csv|text overrides that. ?list=Name is the list to fill (default Imported). It is created if you do not have it; names match without regard to case. In a CSV, a list column per row wins over ?list=. Only name is required in a CSV. A text body takes the checklist lines above or any plain list. At most 500 rows. curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: text/csv" \ --data-binary @costco.csv "$ARYA/lists/import?list=Costco" # {"created":3,"skipped":0,"lists":[{"id":"l-1a2b3c4d","name":"Costco"}]} created is the number of new items. skipped counts rows that were empty, not items, repeated, over the 500 limit, or already on a list. Checked state and department are applied to new items only.

Your own data only: the receipts you filed. Receipts filed by other members of your household group are not returned. Nothing here is inferred by Arya. Totals are sums of what your receipts say. A receipt is {id, merchant, date, total, subtotal, tax, items, reconciles, has_photo}. The detail adds lines: {name, qty, unit_price, line_total, line_type} with line_type item, discount or return (returns are negative). curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$ARYA/receipts?limit=20&offset=0" # newest first, max 200 curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $ARYA/receipts/ext-1a2b3c4d5e curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $ARYA/receipts/ext-1a2b3c4d5e/original > receipt.jpg curl -s -X DELETE -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $ARYA/receipts/ext-1a2b3c4d5e GET /receipts/export?format=csv|json returns every receipt you filed. The CSV has one row per line, with columns receipt_id,merchant,date,name,qty,unit_price,line_total,line_type. /receipts/{id}/original is the photo or PDF you uploaded, if Arya kept one (has_photo). Filing a receipt through the API is not in v1; use the app or the agent connector.

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" $ARYA/analysis/spending # {"trips":2,"spend_total":11.5,"returns_total":4.0, # "by_month":{"2026-10":11.5},"by_store":{"Costco":11.5,"Trader Joe's":0.0}} spend_total adds up the receipt totals. by_store groups by the merchant name printed on the receipt.

What you bought and when, by the name Arya read from the receipt (max 500): {"items":[{"name","times_bought","qty","spent","first_bought","last_bought"}]}, most often bought first. Returns and discounts are not counted as buys.

Errors are JSON, with the matching HTTP status: {"error": {"code": "not_found", "message": "no such list"}} Status code When 400 bad_request a bad or unknown field, bad JSON, bad format 401 unauthorized no token, a wrong token, or a revoked token 404 not_found no such list or item (also for another account's ids) 413 too_large body over 256 KB 429 rate_limited over the hourly limit; see Retry-After 500 internal_error our fault; try again

600 calls per account per hour, shared with the agent connector and every other route a token reaches (ARYA_MCP_RATE). Over it you get 429 with a Retry-After header in seconds. 256 KB per request, 50 items per add call, 500 rows per import.

Not in v1: webhooks, OAuth, sharing a list with another account, filing a receipt, and Quest data. Arya's own inference (what is running low, suggestions, aisle and store maps, prices from other households) is not part of the API on purpose. The API is for your own data.

I built Arya as one well-defended single-server app on purpose. The window was for the product, not for a fleet of servers. This page has three parts: what is built and holds up for a few dozen people at once, what I know is weak, and the plan to grow past that. The dated choices are in the decision log, what was made and when is on the build page, and the unbuilt ideas are in the roadmap. What runs today is in Architecture.
documents.s: Design decisions, and what comes next

documents.t: Code does money, timing and lists at no model cost. The ledger, patterns and derived list are rebuilt from the receipts, with no model involved, so they cannot drift. Every model call goes through one module that enforces the personal-data rule. (Architecture 0.3, 0.4) Safe writes on one box. Atomic JSON writes, a per-file lock, a per-request memo, and a full Postgres copy of every account document on the live site. (Architecture 0.5) Layered spend control. A daily ceiling for the app, a separate one for the demo, a per-visit share, per-account monthly and hourly limits, and an Ops switch to pause paid reads or change the photo reader without a deploy. Every call writes a ledger row. (Model policy) Background work that survives a restart. Receipt batches and store scans keep a pending list on disk and resume after a deploy. Live sync that already spans processes. Shared-list changes use Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY, one listener per process. (Architecture 0.8) A demo that cannot touch real data. Each visit writes to an in-memory sandbox with a size cap. Security basics. Hashed session and token secrets, a strict script CSP, upload caps at the proxy, throttled sign-in, and people pixelated out of shelf photos before anything is stored. Measured. A scale simulator and a read-only performance pass on 2026-11-02. The Today screen takes about 65 ms alone, about 1.1 s with 10 people at once and about 4 s with 30. That was on a development machine, not the live server.

These are the findings from my own architecture audit of 2026-11-01 that still hold. Each is tied to a phase of the scalability design. Two audit items are already closed: /health reports the running commit, and the photo reader is Spark first (see the model map). That second change took the cost pressure off receipt batches. What Why it matters Fixed in One process, one interpreter lock, no cap on model reads in the request thread pool A burst of photo reads can slow pages that never call a model Phases 4 and 6 The spend guard reads the whole ledger file on each paid call; password sign-in hashes on the event loop Both block other requests while they run, and the ledger grows with use Phase 2 for the ledger; the hashing is not in the plan yet Spend checks are "check, then spend", with no reservation Parallel reads can overshoot a limit Phase 6 The ledger is an estimate from a price table, never reconciled with the provider's console What Arya thinks it spent and what was billed can differ Not in the plan yet; a manual weekly check Postgres mode stores documents whole, with no version column or pool Two processes could lose an update silently Phase 2, before any second process Sessions, demo visits, rate buckets and the receipt queue live in memory or files A deploy drops every demo visit Phases 3 and 5 One worker reads every account's receipt batch in order; no cap on batches parked on disk One big import makes the next person wait Phase 5 Store-map photos are base64 in one JSON file rewritten per photo The first wall the simulator found Phase 7 Saves mirror the whole document to Postgres inside the request A slow database slows a list tick Phase 1 restore.sh wipes the data folder before extracting; the off-site backup is set up by hand A bad archive or a lost VM could lose data Phase 0 Tests run in CI only on demand (my choice, to keep the loop fast) A broken merge can reach the server unless someone runs the suite Not a scaling item; revisit after judging Concurrency rules are by convention (each writer must remember the lock) Easy to get wrong as more people touch the code Phase 2

documents.t: Scalability design has nine phases (0 to 8, the numbers the table above uses). Each phase is switched on by settings. Each has a rollback and a number to measure: Baseline: request timing, a metrics endpoint and a live load test. Hot cache: a short-lived cache, and the Postgres mirror off the request path. Postgres master: Postgres as the master copy, with versioned updates. Shared short-lived state: sessions, demo visits and rate buckets in a shared store. Several processes. Queue and workers: a job queue for receipt, scan and reminder jobs. Model gateway: concurrency caps and spend reservation. Object storage for photos. Cloud provider. Versioned writes come before a second process, and nothing runs before judging ends. It is a plan, not a promise.

documents.t: Rule: every job runs on the cheapest model that holds its golden-set score. Escalation is by evidence (a scored eval), never by default.

muse-spark-1.3 Standard: $1.25 in / $0.15 cached / $4.25 out muse-spark-1.3 Contributor: $0.10 in / $0.002 cached / $0.20 out (different data terms; not used). Limit 150 requests/min. Not the app's tier; see "Spark tier" below. muse-wonder-1.0: $4.00 in / $0.20 cached / $20.00 out. This is the expensive frontier model, not a budget tier. It is banned from volume paths. muse-image-1.0: $0.01/image. muse-voice-transcribe-1.0: $0.18/audio-hour. sam-3.1: $2.50 per 1,000 images; $0.20 per 1,000 video frames.

documents.t: The cheapest model is no model. Patterns, cadence, run-out dates, ledger math, reconciliation, and list generation are deterministic code: $0. Volume intelligence (receipt decode fallback, list and date photos, command parsing, Ask Arya, judge): Spark, reasoning_effort=low, stable prefixes cached. Spark runs as muse-spark-1.3 Standard (see "Spark tier" below). Exception (owner, 2026-11-04): the list photo read sends reasoning_effort=minimal for speed, and repeats once at low if the API refuses the value. Eval loops (golden sets, prompt variants): Contributor mode. Gate scores still count on Standard. (Superseded for app traffic by the 2026-11-01 amendment.) Wonder: zero jobs at baseline (history; the live reader is auto, see below). A job earns Wonder only by failing its golden set on Spark at two effort levels, with the eval logged. Voice: transcribe on demand only; Ask has no voice out (replies are text). Muse Image: painted the 23 characters once and paints share looks (live); a dinner render is planned, not built. muse-image-1.0 costs $0.01 per image. It is the one place a flat per-unit price beats token metering.

PDF receipt decode: ~2.9 cents/receipt. Photo: ~1.5 cents short, ~3.1 long. JSON import: $0. Patterns on imported history: $0. Policy targets: a full trip decode at or under 1 to 2 cents; total hackathon API spend well under the $150 credit (plan §8 estimated $57 to $61 at defaults).

documents.t: There is no $0 rule. Hackathon credits (Meta Model API, plus Baseten and Modal) are available, so spending on Meta models (Muse Image, Spark, Wonder, SAM) is allowed when it improves the product or demo. Stay budget-aware: the cheapest model that holds its score is still the default, spend goes through the ledger, and large batches get a capped trial first. The in-code caps (daily and demo budgets) are unchanged.

My decision 2026-11-01: receipt photos are read by the auto reader (Ops "Photo reader" = "Spark first, Wonder as backup"): Spark reads first. Wonder re-reads only when Spark fails or the checks below flag the read (arithmetic, low confidence on too many lines). Wonder stays allowed as that second reader through Nov 9. That is meant to cover judging after submission. The original 2026-10-27 amendment (Wonder first, Spark fallback) is summarized below. Original (2026-10-27): through Nov 4, judge-facing photo decode ran Wonder first with a Spark fallback. Wonder scored 97 of 98 lines after hand adjudication (the automatic scorer gives Wonder 86 of 98) against Spark's 92 of 98 on the automatic scorer. The numbers, latency, cost and the staple-judge check are in WONDER-EVAL.md. Auto reader (built 2026-11-01; my pick for judging on 2026-11-01; NOT yet measured on photos). ARYA_PHOTO_READER=auto (or the Ops "Photo reader" switch) reads with Spark first and runs the checks in api/decode/checks.py (lines add up to the subtotal, subtotal plus tax equals the total, the footer item count, impossible prices, too many unsure lines, a price far from the same item number's earlier price on the account). Only a receipt that fails them is re-read by Wonder. A Spark failure goes straight to Wonder. If Wonder is down, the Spark read is kept and every line is sent to review. The receipt records decoded_by and second_read (the reasons), so it is never silent. Why it exists: Wonder won the eval on accuracy. Spark is about nine times cheaper per receipt and about four times faster. Cheap arithmetic can catch most of Spark's mistakes. Known gap, from the Gate 0 notes: a price rotation (two prices swapped between lines) keeps the sum, so arithmetic alone misses it. The price history check covers it only for item numbers seen before. Before the default changes, run python3 -m harness.photo_reader_eval --photos DIR on the Gate 0 photos and require that every price where Spark and Wonder differ is on a flagged receipt. After Nov 9 the amendment above ends. If I extend it, auto keeps Wonder's accuracy only where the checks say it is needed. Otherwise photo decode is Spark only. Demo budget. Each demo visit may spend ARYA_DEMO_SESSION_BUDGET_USD (code default $0.40; $2 on the live site, owner 2026-11-04) on live reads, held in that visitor's in-memory sandbox; all demo visits together stay under ARYA_DEMO_DAILY_BUDGET_USD (code default $2; $100 a day on the live site for the judging window, about 50 full visits a day, and the top of the Ops range). Ops > Settings > Dollar limits sets both without a deploy and beats the env file. To go back through the env file, set ARYA_DEMO_DAILY_BUDGET_USD=2 and ARYA_DEMO_SESSION_BUDGET_USD=0.40 in the VM env file, then run docker compose up -d in assistant/deploy (a plain restart does not re-read the env file). Switch after Nov 9, not before. The photo reader is an env setting: ARYA_PHOTO_READER=spark in the VM env file, then docker compose up -d in assistant/deploy (not restart, which keeps the old environment), puts photo decode on Spark Standard with no deploy. Unset, or wonder, is the amendment path. Receipts record decoded_by, so the switch is visible in the data. Spark-only photo decode scored 93.88% in the Gate 0 eval, with the review queue as the mitigation.

Spark and Wonder run in Standard mode. Meta's models page (dev.meta.ai/docs/models): "In Standard mode, your content is not used to train Meta models." Earlier on 2026-11-01 I had moved the app's Spark calls to muse-spark-1.3-contributor for the lower price; the same day I moved them back to Standard, so nothing the app sends is used for training. Code: meta_client.resolve_mode() maps the app's "standard" (Spark) mode to the tier set on the Ops screen or in ARYA_SPARK_TIER; the Ops screen setting wins. Wonder is always Standard. An explicit mode="contributor" with personal=True is still refused. Option, not built: a community (Contributor) tier with user opt-in could support more users at lower cost. It needs an opt-in screen, a per-user routing rule and updated privacy text first, and my word. Rate limits: Standard allows 3,000 requests/min per team. The Contributor tier allows 150/min, so meta_client keeps a sliding-window gate at 140/min for that case. A call that would wait over 20 s fails with "Arya's AI is busy right now" (HTTP 502) instead of hanging. Receipt photos follow the auto reader above. SAM, Muse Voice and the open-weights client are unchanged.

A one-time look (2026-11-02) at every model Meta offered me, what Arya uses today, and what it could use later. The models in use are described in assistant/docs/MODEL-POLICY.md and docs/quest/META-PRODUCTS.md. This page adds the models I did not use. The model list comes from Meta's models page (dev.meta.ai/docs/models) as read on 2026-11-02, and the code from assistant/api/meta_client.py. Where I could not confirm something, it says "unconfirmed". Everything under "Future" is an idea, not built and not promised.

documents.t: The best raw material for better store maps and shelf help already exists online: walkthrough videos and in-store photos on YouTube, TikTok and similar sites. Arya cannot use them. They belong to their creators and the platforms, and the platform terms forbid bulk collection. Arya's own rule is that no store map is built from footage I do not have the right to use. The Trader Joe's walkthrough experiment was removed for exactly this reason (see docs/quest/META-PRODUCTS.md). Today every store map comes from a shopper walking their own store with the guided scan. Future idea: a data partnership. A store chain, a licensed-content provider or a platform that can legally supply in-store video and photos (aisle walkthroughs, shelf signs, layout) would let Arya: start each store with a first map instead of an empty one; test and tune the shelf-reading step (SAM plus Spark) on many layouts, not one household's; give community shoppers better "where is it" help from day one. Any partnership would need written permission, store consent, the existing people-pixelating rule, and a takedown route. See docs/ROADMAP.md ("Store data and community").

documents.t: React 19 and TypeScript, built by Vite into web/dist. The API serves the build at / and the static folder assistant/pwa/ (images, store models, three.js, scene.js, the manifest, icons) beside it; the build wins on a name clash. index.html and sw.js are sent with Cache-Control: no-cache. The old address /next/... answers 302 to the same path at /. One screen per file in web/src/screens/, listed in screens/registry.tsx. Navigation is a stack (app/nav.tsx); the session (user, demo, currency, language) is app/session.tsx. Shared parts: web/src/ui/ (sheet, toast, info sheet, the store view) and web/src/lib/ (API calls, formats, stores, language). The hunt, Express, Pack, haul, album, share, mapper, group live sync (app/groupLive.ts), push reminders, powers and the install prompt are ported one to one from the old plain-JS files. The store view is scene.js (three.js), loaded as a classic script. The navigation tab is Today, Spending, Quest, Ask and More (the default; it can be customized). More holds Lists, Receipts, Stores, Help and Settings. Settings opens the Profile page (Group, Preferences with Reminders, Account, About Arya, Sign out last). About Arya is the about view: Arya's powers, Use Arya in Muse, Add to Home Screen, Keeping Arya running. (Updated 2026-11-02, #416; this replaced the earlier six-tab layout.) Service worker web/src/sw.js, built to /sw.js (vite-plugin-pwa, injectManifest). It precaches the built shell and the runtime files of the static folder. It is network first. It sends /api/, /auth/, /decode, /import and /eyes straight to the network, never touches a write (non-GET) or the live stream /api/group/live, and shows push reminders. It takes control at once and deletes every other cache, the old arya-v* caches too. Security: no inline script (the CSP has script-src 'self'; tests/test_csp.py checks web/index.html); no inline handlers. Tests: string pins in assistant/tests/ (they read web/src through tests/frontend.py), vitest tests beside the code (web/src/**/*.test.ts*), and browser runs in web/e2e/. Style: light theme, greyscale structure and one orange accent; see DESIGN.md.

api/state.py keeps one JSON document per former file (receipts, dictionary, flags, lists, quest, push...). ARYA_STORE picks the backend: json (default; files under data/users/<account>/), dual (files are the truth, each save mirrors to Postgres) or pg (Supabase table arya.user_docs, keyed by owner and document name, role arya_app, via DATABASE_URL). The demo account always uses files, and its visitors write only to an in-memory sandbox overlay. Caches and big blobs (shelf_matches.json, storemap_img.json) stay on disk in every mode. A receipt's original photo or PDF is kept per account.

Password accounts (PBKDF2 hashes, throttled sign-in, cookie sessions whose tokens are stored as SHA-256 hashes). Account names allow only letters, digits and . _ % + - @. Email-code sign-in goes through Supabase Auth and Google sign-in is Arya's own (api/google_oauth.py, used when GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID and GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET are set; otherwise Google goes through Supabase). Either way the provider only proves an email address; Arya keeps its own account and cookie (api/supabase_auth.py, flag ARYA_SUPABASE_AUTH). The Muse connector and the Lists API use a bearer token whose hash is stored.

api/prices.py is deterministic and uses only the household's own receipts: per-store unit prices, a cheaper-store hint when the gap is real, a trend only with enough buys over enough days, the household's own basket inflation, a split-the-list suggestion, food waste in dollars. Nothing is fetched from a store, a flyer, an API or the web. Ask Arya answers price questions from these precomputed facts. Community prices, Deals and Arya Shoppers are opt-in, recorded only, and not live.

With ARYA_GROUPS=1 (on in compose), an account in a group reads and writes the shared stores (lists, flags, product knowledge) in the group's plane; receipts stay with the account that filed them and every member sees them. Invites are a 6-letter code valid 48 hours. Leaving copies the lists. Live sync: every shared save calls live.changed(group_id); each open app holds one Server-Sent Events stream (/api/group/live) and reloads when its group changes. With DATABASE_URL set the change is a Postgres NOTIFY arya_group and one listener thread per process wakes its streams; without it, or with ARYA_LIVE_PG=0, the wake stays in-process.

Flag ARYA_PUSH_REMINDERS=1 plus VAPID keys. A phone opts in from Settings; the subscription is saved in push.json. A daily cron line runs python -m api.reminders, which sends at most one push per account per day for staples that run out inside the notice window. No model calls. Steps: PUSH-REMINDERS.md.

One Oracle VM, Docker Compose with two services: api (uvicorn, deploy/Dockerfile.api) and caddy (TLS, security headers, CSP, plain HTTP redirects to HTTPS). Data lives in the arya-data volume. Settings come from deploy/.env (VM only); compose lists every variable the app reads, and tests/test_compose_env.py fails if one is missing. Deploy is git pull then docker compose up -d --build in assistant/deploy (deploy.sh); never rsync --delete. The api image builds the app (web/) in a node stage and copies web/dist in. backup.sh and restore.sh handle the nightly backup. CI is manual only (.github/workflows/tests.yml).

Every model call writes a row to the cost ledger. The app, the demo household and each demo visit spend from separate buckets (§10). Live doors, batch judge runs and hunt creation pass the guard first; the demo's live doors also have per-IP caps. Deterministic code never calls a model. An Ask message the guard refuses costs $0 (no model call), and max_tokens bounds each Ask reply (§6).

Arya has two layers. Each layer does the work it is good at. The edge is the user's own Muse. It sees the media: receipt photos, PDFs, pasted orders. It reads them and sends Arya structured data only; on this path no receipt image reaches the server. A receipt photo filed in the app itself is kept per account and is viewable in the app ("View receipt", Discussion 42). This is an accepted trade-off, recorded in SPEC.md. The core is the Arya server. It verifies, remembers, reasons, and answers. It spends no tokens on reading media. The rule between the layers: the client proposes, Arya disposes. Client data is untrusted. Totals must reconcile in code before a receipt is accepted. Low-confidence lines go to the review queue.

All paths end in one contract: a decoded receipt with lines, subtotal, tax, and total. Structured intake (primary). POST /api/intake/structured. The user's Muse posts the decoded receipt as JSON. The server recomputes every line status. A subtotal that does not match the lines fails reconciliation and is marked, never silently accepted. Order text. POST /api/intake/order-text. A pasted online order (Instacart, Amazon) is extracted server-side, then follows the same path. Delivery fees and tips are excluded by rule. Server decode (fallback). PDF text and photo decode endpoints remain for clients that cannot decode at the edge. They use the Model API under the model policy (MODEL-POLICY.md). Costco JSON export. Bootstrap seed only. It is not a product intake path.

Arithmetic: line totals must sum to the subtotal within 5 cents. Line status: auto at confidence 0.8 or above, else unverified and into the review queue. Discount lines are structure, not identity. A discount line (Costco prints it as "/") attaches to its parent item (named on the receipt, else the previous item line) and is always auto-verified. It never enters the review queue, on any path. Fee lines are classified once and never enter patterns or the list.
documents.s: 3. Verification in code (no model, no cost)

documents.t: Three mechanisms, in order of strength. The dictionary maps each store SKU to a canonical name. A name the user confirms teaches the dictionary. An item whose name cannot be established is unresolved: off the list, out of patterns, waiting in the review queue. Arya never guesses a name. Groups. Products are grouped by an explicit group key when one is set, else by their normalized name. Costco re-SKUs the same product under one name; the group is the product everywhere it matters: patterns, ledger, list. Merges and splits set the explicit key. The Curator (server-side reasoning) proposes merges and splits inside candidate clusters built in code at no cost. The model judges a cluster under a strict doctrine: same product only; never across organic vs conventional, form, flavor, fat content, or a size that makes a different product; when in doubt, keep separate. A proposal changes nothing until the user applies it. No silent edits, ever. Proposals the dictionary has already overtaken (members already one group, a duplicate, a split already in effect) retire automatically as superseded and are never shown.

Arya's server models have no web access. Identification from the outside world is therefore an edge job, run by the user's Muse: Trigger: an unresolved dictionary item, or an unverified receipt line whose name is abbreviated or unreadable. Method: the retailer's own catalog first. A store item number matched on the retailer's site (for Costco: costco.com and its same-day storefront) is the strongest evidence. Then the wider web. Output: candidates with source URLs, posted to Arya (POST /api/review/suggest) and shown in the review queue next to the item or line. Research is evidence, not a verdict: the user settles with one tap, and settling teaches the dictionary. A brand initial alone is not evidence. Items with no catalog match stay open.
documents.s: 5. The Resolver: research at the edge

documents.t: Each agent has a narrow job and a named limit. Staple judge. Input: pattern facts only (buys, cadence, quantities, all computed in code). Output: STAPLE, SEASONAL, OCCASIONAL, ONE_OFF, or NOT_CONSUMABLE per product. The verdict gates admission to the list. Explicit user intent always beats the judge. Unjudged and unresolved items stay off the list. Curator. See §4. Proposes identity changes; never applies them. Ask Arya. Chat over a household snapshot. Actions (add to list, remove from list, ran out, mark expired, never suggest, snooze) are validated server-side. A list is found by a near name ("Costco" finds "Costcozy"), and only a row already on a list can be removed. The snapshot carries receipt facts (count, last, biggest, trips per store), spend per store per month, pack dates as words, and the cheapest store per item. Numbers come from the data, never from the model. At most 10 actions run in a turn. More than 3 removes in one turn wait for a yes (Yes, do these or Not now) on every screen. On the Ask tab the other actions apply at once; from a list or a hunt, adds apply with Undo and the riskier actions (out, expired, never, snooze) wait for a yes (/api/chat/apply). Demo sessions can chat; it is a live door under the demo's per-IP and per-visit caps (§10). Ask guard (api/ask_guard.py). The person's latest message is checked against high-confidence phrases only (an override with a target, a prompt leak, secrets, other accounts). A hit gets a fixed refusal with no model call, and counts a strike. Three strikes in 24 hours pause Ask: a demo visit for 24 hours, a real account until the owner unlocks it in Ops (the message says to email support). The owner is never locked. A reply that quotes the system prompt, holds something shaped like a key or links off Arya is swapped for the refusal, with no strike. Stored text (item and list names, the screen, a photo) never strikes. Each Ask reply is capped at 1,500 tokens.
documents.s: 6. The reasoning agents in the core

documents.t: Returns are first-class: FIFO netting against buys, refunds reconcile into spend, patterns count kept items only, a returned item is never re-suggested. Every line carries an allocation: HOUSEHOLD (default) or FOR-OTHERS. For-others spend is in the ledger, never in patterns, inventory, or the list. The list is a derived view of the inventory model, never the source of truth.
documents.s: 7. Money rules (summary; SPEC.md owns the detail)

documents.t: Per-user state is a set of JSON documents, one per former file (receipts, dictionary, flags, lists, quest...). ARYA_STORE picks where they live: json (files under data/users//, the default), dual (files are the truth, every save is mirrored to Postgres), or pg (table arya.user_docs, see api/pgstore.py). The demo account always stays on files. An account name is also a folder name, so it holds only letters, digits and . _ % + - @ (auth.valid_name). Passwords are PBKDF2 hashes; sign-in is throttled; sessions are cookies, and session tokens are stored as SHA-256 hashes. Email code sign-in (Supabase Auth) is built behind ARYA_SUPABASE_AUTH=1, off by default and on in the live site. Google sign-in is Arya's own (api/google_oauth.py) when its client id and secret are set, with the Supabase Google provider as the fallback. The provider only proves the email; Arya keeps its own account (named by the email, no password) and its own cookie (api/supabase_auth.py). A connector token is arya_ plus a random secret. Only its SHA-256 hash is stored. It is shown once at mint. Minting a new one replaces the old, and it can be revoked at any time. Bearer tokens are accepted alongside session cookies, and the same token works for the Lists API (/api/v1). A token cannot reach paid bulk reads, Ops, groups, push, export or the Kroger lookup (demo_guard._TOKEN_BLOCKED). Demo accounts cannot mint. The Muse connector (custom.arya) carries its own instruction doc: operations, when to file, the verification rules, the Resolver procedure, filing hygiene. The doc is the standing prompt. The user writes no prompt. Routing is contextual. A receipt, an order, or a question about the user's own list, spend, or inventory goes to Arya. A general question does not. "Arya, …" always routes. Ambiguous input: ask, or state the assumption.

Create an account. A new account opens on Today; there is no Connect an AI agent step on first run. Connecting Muse is optional, from Settings > About Arya > Use Arya in Muse: make the code there (shown once). Tell the Muse agent to connect to Arya; it asks for the code and opens a secure credentials vault. Paste the code there, never into a chat message. Talk to Muse. The screen carries these steps and a copyable fallback setup prompt for assistant apps that do not load the connector doc automatically. The Muse Code settings-file route is the backup (AGENT-CONNECTOR.md).

MODEL-POLICY.md is normative: deterministic work in code at $0; Spark 1.3 Standard, low effort, cached prefixes for volume reasoning (if the Contributor operator option is on, a client-side 140 requests/min gate applies; its limit is 150); Wonder is banned from volume paths. Every model call is written to a cost ledger. The app's daily ceiling (ARYA_DAILY_BUDGET_USD, $10) stops app model spend; the demo household spends from a separate bucket (ARYA_DEMO_DAILY_BUDGET_USD, $100/day in compose) and each demo visit from its own share (ARYA_DEMO_SESSION_BUDGET_USD, $2 in compose), so demo use cannot drain the app. Every live door, batch judge run and hunt creation passes the guard first. A model answer that cannot be read is a 502 with a plain sentence, never a 500 (meta_client.parse_json). Each account has its own limits: a monthly heads-up, a monthly pause on paid reads, and an hourly freeze (defaults $3, $5 and $1, see the flag table; the live site uses $3, $20 and $10, and the owner account is exempt), on top of the daily ceiling for the whole app. api/meta_client.py is the only module that calls the Model API. The personal-data rule is enforced there by construction.

One Oracle VM (Always Free; no new cloud resources). Docker Compose: the API and Caddy with Let's Encrypt. No database container: data is JSON files, mirrored to Supabase on the live site (ARYA_STORE=dual); after judging Postgres can become the master copy (pg). Public name: arya.teamnightshift.org (Cloudflare A record, DNS only). The old arya-pilot.duckdns.org name is a permanent Caddy redirect to it. Known limit: one uvicorn process on one VM. Demo sandboxes live in that process's memory and the JSON files have one writer, so it cannot run as several processes yet. Dual-mode saves mirror to Supabase inside the request, so a slow Supabase can slow a save. Roughly a few dozen people at once is the ceiling (README, Known limits). After judging: Postgres as master copy, session state out of memory, several processes, a cloud provider (see docs/ROADMAP.md; the phased design is docs/SCALABILITY-DESIGN.md, a plan, not built). Deploy is git pull on the VM, then a compose rebuild. Never rsync --delete: it once deleted the VM-only deploy environment. Settings come from deploy/.env (VM only). Compose passes only the variables it lists, so every setting the app reads is listed in docker-compose.yml; tests/test_compose_env.py fails if one is missing. .env.example names them. The full test suite runs before a PR merges. A GitHub Actions workflow (.github/workflows/tests.yml) runs it on demand only, not on every PR (my choice). Nothing is committed to main directly; a session log goes to loops/ and STATUS.md is updated.

Log caps. Compose caps each container's log at 5 files of 10 MB (x-logging in docker-compose.yml), so logs cannot fill the disk. The cap applies when a container is recreated: docker compose up -d. Nightly backup. deploy/backup.sh archives the data volume (and the arya Postgres schema when ARYA_BACKUP_DATABASE_URL is set in deploy/.env) into ~/arya-backups, keeping the newest 7 of each. Install once on the VM with crontab -e: 17 3 * * * /path/to/arya/assistant/deploy/backup.sh >> /path/to/arya-backup.log 2>&1 Check it with ls -l ~/arya-backups the next morning. Off-VM copy. A backup on the same disk dies with the VM. Install rclone (sudo apt install rclone), run rclone config once to add a remote you own (Oracle Object Storage, Google Drive, any S3), then add ARYA_BACKUP_REMOTE=<remote>:arya-backups to deploy/.env. The script then copies each night's files there and exits non-zero (so the log shows it) if the copy fails. Restore. deploy/restore.sh <arya-data-*.tar.gz> stops the api, replaces the data volume and starts it again. The Postgres dump is restored by hand with psql.

Per account, in quest.json: sessions, Shop-Offs, friends, Spotter reports, and sightings (item, store, shelf label, time; no image). shelf_frames.json holds one fresh shelf photo per store and item, already scrubbed of people by SAM (shelfscan.scrub_people; no scrub, no frame). GET /api/quest/plan counts purchases per store from the ledger for Plan a hunt ($0). The demo sandbox overlays all of it in memory. The store directory (stores.json) is platform-level.

A fixed per-account spend allowance that resets by itself. Not built; per-account limits do exist (§10: defaults $3 heads-up, $5 pause, $1 hourly freeze; live $3, $20, $10). Public registration is closed by default (ARYA_REGISTRATION_OPEN; the Ops flag overrides the env and is closed on the live site). The owner can open it in Settings. Every door runs on Meta models: Muse in chat, Spark on the Meta API in the app. Forgot-password: not built. Once switched on, email code sign-in (§8) lets a person in without a password.

Status: a plan, not shipped. Nothing on this page is built unless it says "today". Written 2026-11-02 against main after #489. It extends the one-line plan in ROADMAP.md ("Scale out as the community grows") and the Known limits entry in the README. Where this page says more, it does not contradict them. No provider, dates or costs are named. Each phase is chosen when the number of shoppers asks for it. One idea shapes every choice here: Arya is a community app that grows with its users. The design keeps one codebase and one set of product rules (assistant/docs/SPEC.md). The operator turns each phase on with settings, one at a time, with a way back.

One container, one process, one VM, as recorded in assistant/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md sections 0.5, 0.10 and 11. phone (PWA) --https--> CDN / DNS proxy ---> Caddy (TLS) ---> uvicorn, 1 process | FastAPI routes | engines ($0 code) | model client v data volume (JSON per account, photos, caches) Postgres on Supabase (mirror, ARYA_STORE=dual) Meta Model API, Baseten (model calls) Where state lives today, and why each one matters for scale: State Where it lives today Shared across processes? Account documents (receipts, lists, flags, quest, ...) JSON files under data/users/<account>/, mirrored to arya.user_docs in Postgres (dual) No: file locks are per process, mirror is write-only Group documents data/groups/<id>/, same mirror No Sign-in sessions sessions.json plus a parsed copy in process memory Through the file only Demo sessions and sandboxes Process memory (auth._demo_sessions, demo_guard._demo_sandboxes) No Rate-limit and door buckets Process memory (api/deps.py, api/demo_guard.py) No Cost ledger JSON lines file, scanned whole for "spent today" Through the file only Receipt originals, shelf frames, map images Files on the data volume (storemap_img.json is rewritten per photo) No Receipt and scan jobs One worker thread per process, pending list in a file No Group live sync Postgres NOTIFY arya_group (one listener thread per process) Yes, when DATABASE_URL is set Push reminders A daily cron line on the VM n/a

Measured numbers are from the read-only performance pass of 2026-11-02 on a development machine with a 117-receipt account, not the live server (the README says the same). The ordering below is a judgment, not a measurement. One process, one GIL. The Today payload is computed in Python on each read (the derived list, ledger and patterns are rebuilt from receipts, with a per-request memo only). Alone it takes about 65 ms. With 10 people at once the median is about 1.1 s, and with 30 about 4 s. Threads share the interpreter, so more threads do not help. The fix is more processes, which the next three items block. Process memory holds visitor state. Demo sessions, demo sandboxes and rate-limit buckets live in the process. A second process would not see a demo visitor's session. A restart drops every demo visit. Files have one writer. _file_lock is a process-local lock. Two processes writing the same account's lists.json would race. Dual mode mirrors the whole document, so the mirror carries no version and cannot detect a lost update. pg mode (not live) is a whole-document read-modify-write with the same process-local locks. Saves wait for the mirror. In dual mode each save upserts the whole document to Postgres inside the request thread (connect timeout 5 s, one retry). A slow database slows every tick on a list. Model calls share the request thread pool. Reads of receipts, Ask and shelf scans run in the default thread pool beside sync routes. A burst of receipt reads can starve plain page loads, and provider rate limits are handled per call, not per app. Big blobs rewrite on every change. storemap_img.json is rewritten per mapping photo; receipt originals live on one disk; the nightly backup is on the same disk unless ARYA_BACKUP_REMOTE is set. No shared cache. The Today payload is recomputed per request. The per-request memo saves repeat work inside one request only. Observability is logs and /health. There is a cost ledger and an ops digest, but no request timing, no queue depth and no alert.
documents.s: 1.1 Bottlenecks, in the order they will bite

documents.t: The target is plain on purpose: stateless app processes behind a load balancer, one database as the master copy, one shared store for short-lived state, one queue for background work, and one object store for files. Every box below is a role, not a product. phone (PWA) --> CDN / edge cache (static shell, images) | v load balancer (TLS, health checks, sticky nothing) | +------------+------------+------------+ | | | | app proc app proc app proc app proc (N identical, stateless) | | | | +-----+------+-----+------+-----+------+ | | | v v v Postgres shared queue object storage (master copy, key-value (jobs, (receipt originals, per-doc store reminders, shelf frames, map versions, (sessions, model calls) images; private LISTEN/NOTIFY) demo boxes, buckets, signed URLs) rate buckets, hot cache) | v worker procs (same image, no HTTP) | v model gateway (one place for concurrency, retries, provider rate limits, cost ledger rows) | v Meta Model API, Baseten (unchanged) metrics + logs + traces from every box --> one dashboard, a few alerts

Same container image as today, started with N processes behind the load balancer. A process keeps nothing between requests except read caches it can lose. Any process can serve any request, so a crash or a deploy takes one process out, not the site. Health check stays /health; the load balancer stops sending to a process that fails it. Rolling deploys replace processes one at a time, and the in-memory demo state no longer matters because it has moved out (2.3). Code change: none to routes. The seams already exist: state._load/_save, auth.new_session/session_info, demo_guard._demo_sandbox, deps rate buckets, receiptjobs/scanjobs queues, live.changed. Each gets a shared backend behind the same function names.

Today Postgres mirrors files (dual). The target makes it the only writer path (pg), with these additions that pgstore.py does not have yet: A version per document. user_docs gains a version integer. A save sends the version it read, and the update is where version = $read. Zero rows means someone else saved first. The request then re-reads, re-applies and retries a few times, then fails plainly. This replaces the process-local file lock and is the one change that makes several processes safe. Connection pool. One pool per process with a small cap, instead of one connection per thread. Timeouts short, so a slow database degrades a request, never hangs a worker. Rows for the things that are not documents. Sessions, the cost ledger, job state and the pending lists become ordinary tables, so "spent today" is one indexed sum, not a whole-file scan. Stockout reports, friends and store maps can follow later (stage 2 in assistant/loops/2026-10-28-supabase-seam.md); they can stay as documents for a long time. Group live sync keeps LISTEN/NOTIFY; with N processes each holds one listener, which is already how live.py is written. Migration from JSON, in order, each step reversible: Keep dual. Add version with a default of 0 and the versioned update path behind a flag; files remain the truth. Nothing observable changes. Re-run assistant/tools/migrate_json_to_pg.py, compare every document (it reports mismatches), and fix any drift. Back up both sides (backup.sh already dumps the schema when ARYA_BACKUP_DATABASE_URL is set). Flip ARYA_STORE=pg on one process while the others stay on dual reads only if the versioned path is on. Otherwise flip the whole site in a quiet hour. Keep writing files for a while as a shadow copy (a new pg+shadow mode, or the same dual logic with Postgres first and the file second) so rollback is a flag flip, not a restore. Stop the shadow file writes once a full backup cycle has passed with no mismatch. From here the files are a backup format, not a store. Rollback at any step: set ARYA_STORE back one mode and redeploy. Before step 4 the files are current; after step 4 rollback means restore the latest file export from the database (a small export tool is part of the phase, see 4).

Sign-in sessions move to a table or the key-value store, keyed by the token hash, with the expiry as a TTL. session_info reads one key. The parsed-file cache (_SESSIONS_SEEN) goes away; a short per-process cache with a TTL of seconds is fine. Demo sessions and sandboxes move to the key-value store with a TTL of one visit (hours), keyed by the demo cookie. The sandbox overlay is already a dict keyed by file path with a 2 MB cap, so it serialises as one value per visit. Reads load the overlay once per request; writes save it back at the end of the request. This is the change that lets a demo visit survive a deploy and lets two processes serve one visitor. Rate-limit and door buckets move to the same store with atomic increments and TTLs, so a cap of "240 door hits per IP per hour" holds across processes. Keep the in-process path as the fallback when no shared store is set, so a laptop run (compose.yaml) and the tests stay as they are.
documents.s: 2.3 Session and demo state in a shared store

documents.t: Today: one worker thread per process for receipt batches and store scans, with a pending list in a file, and a cron line for reminders. Target: a queue with named job types (receipt.read, scan.read, reminders.daily, backup.nightly, export.account) and worker processes that run the same code as today's thread loops. A job carries the account, a lease and a retry count. A crashed worker's lease expires and another worker picks the job up. Idempotency keys (the job id plus the frame number, which receiptjobs already uses) make a retry safe. Reminders become a scheduled job that enqueues one reminders.account job per opted-in account. A slow push to one phone then does not delay the rest, and the cron line on the VM goes away. The "Your receipts are ready" and "Your map is ready" cards keep polling the job list exactly as now; only the producer of that list changes.

Every model call already goes through api/meta_client.py (and open_client.py for the open model). The target puts a small gateway behind those two modules: a per-model concurrency cap, a per-provider token-bucket for the published request limits, retries with backoff on 429 and 5xx, and a timeout per job kind (Wonder re-reads are long, Ask is short). Interactive calls (Ask, a single receipt from the camera) keep a reserved share of the concurrency so a batch upload never blocks a question. Batch calls (bulk receipt reads, scans, judge runs, dictionary enrichment) go through the queue (2.4) and the gateway's batch share. Budgets stay as they are in policy (ARYA_DAILY_BUDGET_USD, demo buckets, per-account limits); their counters move to the database (2.2) so they hold across processes. A spend reservation is taken before the call and settled after, so two processes cannot both spend the last dollar. The ledger row per call stays the audit record; the gateway writes it.
documents.s: 2.5 Model calls: one gateway, queued, rate-limited

documents.t: Three layers, each safe to lose: Edge. The built shell and static images already carry immutable cache headers; the CDN serves them. Nothing under /api/ is cached at the edge. Shared hot cache. The Today payload per account (and per group plane) is cached in the key-value store for a few seconds and dropped on any save to that account or group (save_at is the one choke point, so the invalidation is one line). The same for the price facts and the derived list. This is the cheapest win on bottleneck 1 and needs no process change; the per-request memo stays as the last layer. Per-process. Short TTL caches for sessions and settings. Rule: cache derived data only. Receipts, lists and flags are read from the master copy, never from a cache, on a write path.

Receipt originals, shelf frames and map images move to a private bucket, one key per account and file (users/<account>/receipts/<id>.<ext>), with signed, short-lived URLs for "View receipt". The database row keeps the key, the size and a content hash. storemap_img.json stops being one rewritten blob: each image is its own object and the map document keeps keys only. Uploads keep going through the API (the people-scrubbing step must run before anything is stored, as today); the API streams the result to the bucket. Deletion of an account deletes its prefix. Backups: the bucket has versioning or a nightly copy to a second bucket; the database dump is the other half. restore.sh restores the volume today and would restore the dump plus point at the bucket.

Metrics per process: request count and latency by route (p50, p95), in-flight requests, thread pool queue length, database pool wait, cache hit rate, queue depth and job age by type, model calls by model with latency, error and 429 counts, spend per bucket. Exposed on a /metrics endpoint the load balancer does not route to the public. Logs: one JSON line per request with a request id, account hash (not the name), route, status, duration and the job id when one applies. The same id goes into model calls and ledger rows. Traces: optional; a request id in logs covers most of what a trace would, until there are several services. Alerts, few and plain: /health red for a few minutes; p95 of /api/today above a line; queue age above a line; model error rate above a line; daily spend near the ceiling. The existing ops digest (harness/ops.py) becomes a reader of the same metrics. Privacy: no receipt content, no names and no photos in logs or metrics; the people-scrubbing and personal-data rules in meta_client stay the boundary.

Each phase is turned on by settings on the current image, has a measurement that says whether it worked, and has a rollback that is a flag flip or a redeploy of the previous image. Phases go in this order because each one removes the blocker for the next. None has a date. Phase What changes Blocker it removes Rollback What to measure 0. Baseline Add request timing and a /metrics endpoint; run the Today load script against the live site in a quiet hour; set ARYA_BACKUP_REMOTE and prove one restore off the VM Nothing is known about the live ceiling Remove the endpoint p50 and p95 of /api/today at 1, 10, 30 concurrent on the live server; restore time 1. Hot cache Today, price facts and derived list cached per plane for a few seconds, invalidated on save; mirror writes moved off the request path (a background queue in-process, with a circuit breaker on failure) Bottlenecks 1 (partly), 4 and 7 Flag off the cache; flag off the async mirror Same load test: median at 10 and 30 concurrent; cache hit rate; save latency with the mirror slow or down 2. Postgres master version column and versioned updates; connection pool; sessions and ledger as tables; pg with shadow file writes; then shadow off Bottleneck 3 and the one-writer rule ARYA_STORE back one mode; restore from files until shadow is off Mismatch count from the migration check (must be 0); lost-update retries per hour; database pool wait 3. Shared short-lived state Demo sessions, sandboxes and rate buckets in a shared key-value store, with the in-process path as fallback Bottleneck 2 Unset the store address; the process path returns A demo visit survives a deploy; door caps hold across two processes 4. Several processes Start N processes behind the load balancer on the same VM first, then on more than one machine; rolling deploys Bottleneck 1 N back to 1 p50 at 30 concurrent falls in step with N; zero demo visits dropped during a deploy 5. Queue and workers Receipt, scan and reminder jobs on the queue; worker processes; cron line retired Bottleneck 5 (partly) ARYA_*_JOBS_INLINE style flags back to the thread loop Job age p95; retries; jobs lost on a worker restart (must be 0) 6. Model gateway Concurrency caps, provider rate buckets, spend reservation, interactive reserve Bottleneck 5 Caps to unlimited; reservation off 429s per hour; Ask latency while a batch runs; spend over the ceiling (must be 0) 7. Object storage Originals, frames and map images in a bucket; storemap_img.json split Bottleneck 6 Keep files on the volume until the copy is verified; read from the volume on a bucket miss Bytes on the volume; map save latency; signed-URL errors 8. Cloud provider Move the whole set (processes, database, store, queue, bucket) to a provider with managed versions of each; the VM becomes a fallback until a full week passes Hardware ceiling DNS back to the VM Same dashboard, same alerts, same load test Phases 0 and 1 can happen on the current VM with no new service. Phase 2 uses the database that already exists. Phase 3 is the first new service. From phase 4 on, the choice of provider matters, and the design above lets any of them fit.

Risk Answer Lost updates when two processes save one document Versioned updates (2.2) before any second process (phase 2 before 4). Never the other order. A migration that silently drops a document The migration tool already counts mismatches; phase 2 requires zero before pg, and shadow file writes keep a second copy. Demo visits dropped during judging Not a risk here: no phase runs before judging ends. Later, phase 3 removes it. Cost spike from more processes The budgets are per app, not per process, once counters live in the database (phase 2) and a reservation exists (phase 6). Until then, run one process. Privacy rules weaken as state moves Each move keeps the same boundary: scrub before store, hashes not names in sessions and logs, personal data only to Meta Standard mode as recorded in AGENTS.md. A phase that touches photos (7) needs a privacy review first. Vendor lock-in Every box is a role with a plain interface (SQL, key-value with TTL, a queue with leases, object keys with signed URLs). Nothing uses a provider-only feature. More moving parts than one person can run Each phase stays optional and off by default; a laptop run and the tests keep the in-process path. The dashboard and alerts (2.8) come in phase 0, before anything else. Reads stay slow because the engines are Python The hot cache (phase 1) and N processes (phase 4) are the first answers. Precomputing the derived state on save instead of on read is a later option the memo design already allows.

documents.t: The product rules, the engines in code at $0, the one model client, the cost policy, the privacy boundary, the PWA, the connector and the API. A shopper would not see a phase happen, except that Today loads as fast with hundreds of neighbours as it does alone today.

So quote the gap between the models, not either number alone. The live reader (auto: Spark first, Wonder re-reads a flagged receipt) is not yet measured on photos. documents.t: Set Lines correct / labeled Accuracy vs 90% gate Public set (identity metric) 90 / 98 91.84% PASS Public set (strict-string metric) 80 / 98 81.63% FAIL Combined: my subset (32/32) + public (identity) 122 / 130 93.85% PASS Combined (strict-string) 112 / 130 86.15% FAIL Two metrics are reported because the task rule ("product identity matches the printed identity, allowing spacing/case differences only") and the decode prompt pull in opposite directions. The SYSTEM prompt itself tells the model to expand brand abbreviations when confident (GG = Green Giant is its own example). The identity metric counts a line correct when the decoded product is the same product as printed (abbreviation expansions such as Bh to Boar's Head, BC to Betty Crocker, KS to Kirkland Signature, and word reordering from the brand/product/detail field split are accepted) and the paid price is exact. The strict-string metric accepts only spacing and case differences. All 10 lines that separate the two metrics are abbreviation expansions, and nothing else. Recommendation: judge the gate on the identity metric. A strict-string gate would penalize behavior the prompt orders. Note: if my subset's 32/32 was scored strict-string, the two subsets are not comparable, and the combined strict figure (86.15%) is the conservative reading.

All public-set data lives ONLY under ~/workspace/meta-hackathon-2026/spike2/public-set/ (photos/, labels/, results/, plus decode_public.py, score_public.py, and this report). The only files on my side read were spike2/decode_photo.py and spike2/run_one.py (to reuse the exact SYSTEM prompt and call pattern) and my subset's result line in spike2/SPIKE2-REPORT.md (4 receipts, 32/32) for the combined figure. Nothing was written to spike1/, spike2/photos/, or spike2/results/. No public item entered any dictionary, ledger, or pattern file. No shared state exists between calls.

Target was 16 public receipts; 9 were obtained (98 labelable lines). The limit was whether the lines could be labeled by hand, not search effort (about 25 image searches plus dataset, archive, and blog sweeps). Real receipts that were found but rejected because the labels could not be trusted: Trader Joe's, 26 items, $52.18: the holder's thumb and a fold cut off the left edge of nearly every product name. Only about 4 lines could be labeled as printed. Fred Meyer (Kroger banner), 15 items, $60.69: photographed at an angle. The item text was too small to transcribe reliably after rotation and upscaling. Target, ~7 lines, about $123.90: skewed photo, item names not reliably readable. Costco (Roseville) and a second Costco photo: thumbs hide the product names. CVS/Walgreens photos found were coupon tails only (no item lines); one WIC slip showed quantities without prices and part of a card number (skipped on both grounds). Rejected outright: fake/AI sample receipts, rendered samples, non-US receipts (Canada, UK, Serbia, Russia, Australia, Colombia), staged prop receipts, and photos too blurry to label. Mix targets. Long receipts (15+ lines): target 4, got 1 (Alexander's, 27 lines); the other long candidates above could not be labeled. Chains beyond Safeway: target 3, got 8. Adverse conditions: hand-held (pub-01, 03, 08, 09), crumpled and rotated 90° (pub-02, kept in original orientation), faded (pub-04, 06), dark and thumb-occluded (pub-08, 09): covered.

Product wrong: 5 (all pub-04, faded vintage print). Digit and code misreads inside abbreviated strings: CHRY48 read as CHRY8, 8PK as SPK, 1884 as 18&4, T/HOUSE16BN as 168N, 96ZPP499 as 962PP499. Four of five carried needs_user_check. All five prices were exact. Price wrong: 3 (all pub-05), a three-way price rotation: ORANGE JUICE 8.99 read as 3.99, NAPOLITANER 2.99 as 4.05, PIZZA POCKETS 4.05 as 7.99. The rotation keeps the line sum, so the arithmetic check alone would not catch it. The ORANGE JUICE error was high-confidence (0.9, no check flag). It is the one silent error in the set. Item-number wrong: 3 of 46 checked (reported separately, not in the pass mark): Walmart RED BELL …4688KF read as …4680KF; Westside BOUNTY …81539 as …81599, and NAPOLITANER 0765600721 as 07858000721. Missed lines: 0. Extra lines: 0. The model emitted exactly the label line count on all 9 receipts, including the 10 label-unreadable lines on the two partial receipts, which it returned as partial reads with needs_user_check (excluded from scoring, not counted as extra). Arithmetic match: 7/7 receipts where a total is in frame (decoded line sum within 0.05 of the subtotal, and decoded total equal to the printed total). pub-08/pub-09 are not scorable (totals out of frame); on both, the model reported the visible-line sum as its total. Conventions and notes: Savings folds were handled correctly everywhere they occur: pub-02 (0.50, 0.68), pub-03 (25%-off line: list 9.32 / paid 6.99 / discount 2.33), pub-09 (Costco instant savings folded into CRNCHMASTER: paid 5.99, discount 2.00). The pub-09 label records the printed line amount (7.99); the line is scored correct under the established spike-1/spike-2 fold convention, with the 2.00 carried in the discount field. items_sold matched the label on all 3 receipts that print it (pub-01: 14, pub-03: 12, pub-06: 3). Where not printed, the model inferred a count (pub-02: 10, pub-04: 27, pub-05: 14) instead of returning null. Harmless here, but worth a prompt note. pub-07: the model duplicated the brand token into the product field (a schema artifact); identity was unaffected under token-set comparison. Decode cost: 72,344 tokens total for 9 photos (23,379 prompt + 48,965 completion).

In three lines. Of the 52 items the staple judge admitted to the list on my 114 receipts, 41 (79%) are staples by purchase cadence alone. No human labels, no model calls, $0. The 11 others are mostly slow-cycle items bought 3 times; one is a clear error. The figure moves with the proxy's definition (0.98 with a looser bar, 0.63 with a stricter one), so quote it with the definition, for one household. Headline: precision 0.79 (41 of 52). One-sentence definition the submission may quote: "Of the 52 items Arya's staple judge admitted to the self-writing list, 41 (79%) were independently corroborated as behavioral staples by purchase cadence alone (bought on at least 4 separate receipts spanning at least 3 different months, returns netted), with no human labels involved." Quotable form: "Judge precision 79% against a cadence-derived ground truth (41/52 admits corroborated); the 11 uncorroborated admits are dominated by slow-cycle consumables bought 3 times, and only one admit (Reynolds Foil, 2 buys 703 days apart) is a clear error."

Data. My live state, copied read-only from the Oracle VM (Docker volume arya-data, per-user dir): 114 real Costco receipts, 2023-10-25 to 2026-10-26; the dictionary (458 entries); and judged.json, the judge's cached verdicts. No model calls were made; spend $0. Identical pipeline. The analysis re-ran the app's own code on the copies: ledger build (discounts folded, fee SKUs excluded), dictionary grouping (Curator merges applied), and the pattern engine's returns netting (FIFO, kept quantity only, FOR-OTHERS lines excluded). Item identities are therefore exactly the identities the judge saw. Admitted set. Items whose cached verdict has list_ok = true (class STAPLE, or SEASONAL). 156 raw verdicts collapse to 155 distinct grouped items under the current group map (one Curator merge); 52 of them are admitted (43 STAPLE, 9 SEASONAL). Ground-truth proxy (behavioral staples). An item is a proxy staple if, after returns netting, it was bought on ≥ K distinct receipts spanning ≥ M distinct calendar months. Primary setting K=4, M=3. Justification: the corpus holds ~3 receipts/month over 36 months, so 4 separate trips in 3 different months is the weakest pattern that excludes one-trip stock-ups, gift/event buys, and two-trip trials, while still catching a quarterly Costco rhythm. The judge's own eligibility bar is 2 buys, so the proxy is deliberately stricter than the judge: it corroborates the judge's rule but does not re-derive it. Metrics. Precision = admitted ∩ proxy / admitted. Recall = admitted ∩ proxy / proxy. Disagreements are listed by name below; the names matter more than the decimals. What this number is NOT. It is not accuracy against a hand-labeled gold set, because no such set exists for this household. It measures agreement between a reasoning judge and an independent cadence proxy. Where they disagree, either can be right. The disagreement lists say which, case by case.

Proxy Proxy staples Precision (all admits) Precision (STAPLE only) Recall K=3, M=2 88 51/52 = 0.98 0.98 0.58 K=4, M=3 (primary) 55 41/52 = 0.79 0.74 (32/43) 0.75 (41/55) K=6, M=4 35 33/52 = 0.63 0.65 0.94 At the primary setting: all 9 SEASONAL admits are corroborated (9/9). Every disagreement below is at K=4, M=3.

Ten of the eleven miss the bar by exactly one receipt or one month. All eleven are slow-cycle or short-window items where the judge's stated reason is plausible on its face: Three buys, three months (7): Avocados; Hand Wash; Kirkland Signature Bodywash; Kirkland Signature Pink Salt; Lubriderm; Organic 2% Milk; Power Up Mega Omega Trail Mix. Soap, lotion, salt and foil are bought rarely because they last; a cadence bar built for food under-counts them. Avocados (Nov 2023 to Jan 2024, then nothing) is the weakest of this group in hindsight. Four buys inside two months (3): Kirkland Signature Butter Quarters, Kirkland Signature Organic Whole Milk, Mini Cukes: a real rhythm of about once every two weeks in Nov and Dec 2023 that does not reappear under the same SKUs later in the corpus (bought elsewhere, or re-SKU'd). The one clear error (1): Reynolds Foil (printed "Reynlds Foil" on the receipt): 2 buys, 703 days apart, judged STAPLE ("long-life foil rebought"). It is also the only uncorroborated admit under the looser K=3, M=2 proxy.

documents.t: All fourteen carry the class OCCASIONAL, and every judge reason cites gap irregularity: Buter Croiss (5 receipts), Cantaloupe (6), KS Lightly Breaded Chicken Breast Chunks (5), KS Pine Nuts (4), KS Pistachio (5), KS Towel (5), KS Walnuts (6), Mixed Pepper (4), Nmcholstoff+ (4), Organic Broc 2Lb (4), Organic Brussels (4), Organic Gre Bean (4), Pumpkin Seed (5), Red Onions (4). None were left unjudged. The judge saw all of them and declined. This is the product's stated policy made visible (precision over recall: a missed item costs the user one tap, an unnecessary suggestion costs trust). Twice-a-year pantry goods (walnuts, pistachios, pine nuts, pumpkin seeds) are the arguable cases: a human might call them staples; the judge calls a 150 to 250 day median gap "occasional," and under its own prompt that is a defensible call.

documents.t: Flags: my state has no flags.json. I have recorded no list edits (no "never suggest", no dismissals, no manual adds) against the judge's output. There is therefore no me-vs-judge settlement signal to report; absence of overrides is noted, not scored. The live list: the cart prepared from the current smart list holds 5 items. The 4 pattern-surfaced items (Organic Raspberry, Mandarins, Kirkland Signature Almonds, Slice Almond, the list that went from 16 to 4 in the first judge sweep) are all corroborated proxy staples at the primary setting (4/4). The fifth, Power Up Mega Omega Trail Mix, is judge-admitted (STAPLE, 3 buys at a 23-day median gap) and sits in the proxy-miss group above by one month of spread. My behavior (it is on my active list, qty 2) sides with the judge.

The precision figure depends on the definition, by construction. Loosen the proxy to K=3, M=2 and precision rises to 0.98, with recall falling to 0.58 (the judge is far more selective than a loose cadence bar). Tighten it to K=6, M=4 and precision falls to 0.63, because a heavier proxy excludes mid-frequency items the judge reasonably admits. K=4, M=3 was fixed before the results were seen, as the weakest bar that still excludes stock-ups and trials; 0.79 is quoted with that definition attached, never bare.

documents.t: One household, one retailer (Costco), 114 receipts. Staples bought at other stores are invisible to both the judge and the proxy. Verdicts are cached at the buy-count current when judged (re-judging triggers at +2 buys); the proxy uses final corpus counts. A verdict can therefore predate an item's later purchases. This cuts against the judge in the recall direction only. Grouping is the Curator's current grouping; a wrong merge would move both sets together, so grouping errors mostly cancel in precision. SEASONAL admits are month-gated in the live list logic; this eval scores the judge's list_ok, which is the judge's own decision, not the seasonal gate's. Analysis: analysis script and state copies are kept out of the repo (my data).

Headline: on the Gate 0 public set, Wonder reads receipts more accurately than Spark. Its errors are the kind the system catches, while Spark's worst error is the kind it cannot. Wonder costs about 9 times more per receipt and takes about 4 times longer. One-sentence result the submission may quote: "On the 9 public Gate 0 receipt photos (98 hand-labeled lines), Muse Wonder 1.0 scored 97/98 lines correct on identity+price against Spark 1.3 Standard's 92/98, with zero price errors and zero silent errors; Spark repeated the set's one known silent failure (a price rotation on Westside Market's receipt, read at 0.85 confidence with no check flag), while Wonder read that line correctly at 0.95." Quotable form: "Wonder 98.98% vs Spark 93.88% identity+price (hand-adjudicated under the Gate 0 definition); price errors 0 vs 4; silent errors 0 vs 4; arithmetic 7/7 both. Latency: Wonder mean 34.4 s vs Spark 8.6 s per receipt photo. Cost: $0.118 vs $0.013 per receipt."
documents.s: Spark vs Wonder on receipt decode: accuracy and latency

documents.t: Data. The Gate 0 public set only: 9 receipt photos (~/workspace/meta-hackathon-2026/spike2/public-set/photos/), 98 hand-labeled lines, labels written before any decode ran. No receipts of mine anywhere in this eval. Identical conditions. Both models ran the app's own photo pipeline: the system prompt from assistant/prompts/decode_photo_v1.md loaded the way api/decode/service.py: load_photo_prompt() loads it, the same message shape as decode_photo(), temperature 0.1, one stateless call per receipt. Spark ran at the app's production configuration (muse-spark-1.3, reasoning_effort=low, the meta_client.chat default). Wonder ran at its default (muse-wonder-1.0, no reasoning_effort sent). This compares the configurations the app would actually ship, and the asymmetry is deliberate: effort is part of a model's production configuration. Scoring, two columns. Gate 0's verdicts were hand-made under a written definition (identity = same product as printed, prompt- sanctioned abbreviation expansions preserve identity, price exact with the savings-fold allowance). This eval first ran an automatic scorer (wonder_score.py) implementing that definition; the scorer was calibrated until it reproduced every Gate 0 hand verdict on the recorded Spark run exactly (90/98 identity, 80/98 strict, same error lines, arithmetic 7/7). The automatic column is that scorer, unmodified, on both fresh runs. Because the scorer's expansion table covers the abbreviations the recorded Spark run used, every automatic non-correct line in both fresh runs was then hand-adjudicated under the same written Gate 0 definition. That is the adjudicated column. Each ruling is listed by name below. Reporting only the automatic column would penalize Wonder for doing what the prompt instructs (expanding abbreviations); reporting only the adjudicated column would hide the judgment calls. Both are printed. Latency is wall-clock per API call, one run, sequential calls. Cost is computed from each response's usage block at the MODEL-POLICY prices (Spark Standard $1.25/$4.25, cached $0.15; Wonder $4/$20 per 1M) via the repo's own estimate_cost. Judge spot check. 20 synthetic grouped items with expected verdicts set from the judge prompt's rules, mirroring the production judge-eval archetypes (weekly staples, December eggnog, twice-a-year spices, gift cards, and the 2-buys-703-days-apart foil case). Run through the app's own api/judge.py batch path, one call per model. Synthetic because the real judge inputs are my purchase history; no personal data was sent to either model.

It cannot show that Wonder judges better.

pub-05, the price rotation. All four of Spark's price errors are on this one receipt, and Wonder made none, here or anywhere. ORANGE JUICE $8.99 read as $3.99 (confidence 0.85, no check flag); ROYAL GALA $5.99 as $2.99 (0.80, no flag); NAPOLITANER $2.99 as $4.05 (0.50, flagged); PIZZA POCKETS $4.05 as $10.99 (0.40, flagged). Wonder read all four at their true prices, 0.88 to 0.95 confidence. The ORANGE JUICE line is the same line that was Gate 0's one silent error in the recorded run: a rotation preserves the line sum, so the arithmetic check (7/7 for both models) cannot catch it. This is the most dangerous error class in the product, and in this run Spark produced it twice silently (0.85 and 0.80, at or above the app's 0.8 auto threshold, so both would auto-post) and Wonder produced it zero times. pub-04 idx16, SNK FRT/S CHRY48 (faded dot-matrix): Spark read "CHRY 8", dropping the 4, at 0.82 confidence and unflagged, so it would auto-post as the wrong product. Wonder read CHRY48 correctly and still flagged the line for a user check (0.58), the correct behavior on a hard line.
